nitpick

```suggestion
    uint64_t index = 0;
```

Any reasoning for doing this?  native ints run "faster" for counters as far as I'm aware, and there's no expectation this can come anywhere close to overflow, so I'm a little confused at the suggestion.

`uint32_t` would also work i guess.

Fixed width types are more explicit and we do not need values < 0 for an index.

I'll mark this as resolved.

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/18795453/why-prefer-signed-over-unsigned-in-c

has some good reading on the topic: "Use signed integers unless you need two's complement arithmetic or a bit pattern"

There's some subtle optimization things that int allows that I will fully admit I don't understand.
@alexander.hansen@9elements.com Does the above make sense for you?

I would say 

https://kevinmahoney.co.uk/articles/my-principles-for-building-software/#make-invalid-states-unrepresentable

is the reason i use unsigned in such situations. It makes it so the variable can only have 'wrong' state in one direction - not both. I simplifies comparisons sometimes.

Otherwise https://github.com/openbmc/docs/blob/master/cpp-style-and-conventions.md#misc-guidelines also applies here, right?

> Always use size_t or ssize_t for things that are sizes, counts, etc. You
need a strong rationale for using a sized type (ex. uint8_t) when a size_t
will do.

Because `index` is an off-by-one count.

I don't care much about it so we might as well keep it as is.
